analysis.one_liner: Caps greenhouse gas emissions through a trading system and invests in clean energy, consumer rebates, and worker training.
analysis.headline: The Senate's cap-and-trade climate bill cleared the Environment and Public Works Committee, was placed on the Senate calendar in February 2010, and never came up for a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have set up a cap-and-trade system: the government caps total greenhouse gas emissions, issues a shrinking number of permits (allowances) that companies must hold for every ton they emit, and lets companies trade those allowances. It targeted an 80% cut from 2005 emissions by 2020 and 83% by 2050. Money from selling and allocating allowances would have gone to consumer refunds for low- and moderate-income households, job training and transition aid for workers, building retrofits, clean vehicle technology, carbon capture for coal plants, nuclear research, and farming and forestry projects that store carbon. The committee approved it, but the full Senate never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and moderate-income households would receive consumer rebates and energy refunds to offset higher energy prices. Workers in energy, construction, and manufacturing would gain training programs, a green construction careers demonstration project, and climate change adjustment assistance for those displaced. Building owners would get retrofit assistance; farmers and forest owners would be paid for carbon-sequestering projects; and the public would get the emissions reductions, plus a new FERC Office of Consumer Advocacy representing energy customers in rate proceedings. Auction proceeds would also flow to deficit reduction.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Households, workers, and clean energy sectors

how_it_helps.text: It requires annual regulations cutting emissions from capped sources to 80% of 2005 levels by 2020, 58% by 2030, and 17% by 2050, with a federal greenhouse gas registry to track the emissions.
Auction proceeds fund a Consumer Rebate Fund for affected consumers and an Energy Refund Account to offset energy cost impacts on low- and moderate-income households.

It creates climate change worker adjustment assistance for workers displaced by the Act, an Energy Efficiency and Renewable Energy Worker Training Fund, a Worker Transition Fund, and a Green Construction Careers demonstration project aimed at middle-class careers.

It establishes the Retrofit for Energy and Environmental Performance (REEP) program, offering loans and financial assistance to retrofit existing homes and buildings for energy efficiency, plus national building efficiency codes and residential water-efficiency incentives.

It sets new greenhouse gas standards for heavy-duty vehicles, requires states and metro planning organizations to set transportation emission targets with 80% federal cost-share grants, and funds clean vehicle manufacturing facility conversions.

It pays owners of agricultural, abandoned mine, and forest land for projects that measurably increase carbon sequestration, and funds flood control, wildfire risk reduction, and water system adaptation in communities facing climate impacts.

It creates an Office of Consumer Advocacy at the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to represent energy customers in rate and service proceedings, and deposits some auction proceeds into a Deficit Reduction Fund.

analysis.who_pays: Power plants, oil refiners, natural gas distributors, and industrial sources that would need to buy or hold emission allowances, plus manufacturers facing new coal-plant performance standards. Some costs would pass through to consumers as higher energy prices, though the bill redirects substantial allowance value back to electricity, natural gas, and heating fuel customers, and to low- and moderate-income households specifically.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy industry

drawbacks.text: Capping emissions would raise the price of electricity, natural gas, and transportation fuels. The bill's own Consumer Rebate Fund and Energy Refund Account exist to offset those increases for low- and moderate-income households, which is an acknowledgment that the costs would be real and fall first on energy bills.

Covered entities could collectively satisfy up to 2 billion tons of their annual compliance obligation with offset credits rather than actual allowances. Offsets are reductions claimed elsewhere, and their quality is hard to verify, so heavy offset use could let emissions continue while the paper targets were met.

A large share of the emission allowance value would be handed out free to industry — energy-intensive trade-exposed sectors, merchant coal units, refineries, and local gas distribution companies — rather than auctioned, which reduces the money available for consumer refunds and deficit reduction and blunts the price signal the cap is meant to create.

Coal-dependent regions and energy-intensive manufacturers argued the compliance costs would damage their competitiveness; the bill responds with a ten-year phase-out of industry rebates beginning in 2026, but the underlying cost to those sectors and their workers is real.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cap-and-trade structure is the most direct tool available for cutting economy-wide emissions, and this version was built to soften the blow on households: consumer rebates and energy refunds for low- and moderate-income families, transition aid for displaced workers, and rebates for trade-exposed manufacturers. The honest drawbacks are that a large share of the allowance value was given free to industry rather than auctioned for consumers and deficit reduction, that up to 2 billion tons a year of obligations could be met with offsets whose real-world integrity is hard to guarantee, and that energy price increases would still be felt by households not fully covered by refunds. A good-faith opponent would also note the cost borne by coal-dependent regions and energy-intensive manufacturers; the bill's own rebate and phase-out provisions are the acknowledgment of that cost.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate environment committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate calendar in February 2010, but the Majority Leader never brought it to the floor for a vote, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 30, 2009 and read twice before being referred to the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works.
The committee held three days of hearings on October 27, 28, and 29, 2009.
After markup sessions on November 3, 4, and 5, 2009, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute.
On February 2, 2010, the committee reported the bill by Senator Boxer with a written report (No. 111-121), and additional and minority views were filed.
The same day, the bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 267 — the waiting list for bills awaiting floor action.
No further action was taken through the end of the 111th Congress on January 3, 2011; the bill never received a vote on the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers, utilities, and other covered emitters are better off because the bill never came to a vote — they avoided the emission caps, allowance obligations, and coal-plant performance standards it would have imposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers and utilities facing the cap

for.name: John Kerry
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 30, 2009 and led the push for Senate passage of cap-and-trade climate legislation.

for.name: Barbara Boxer
for.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
for.what_they_did: Chaired the hearings and markup, and reported the bill to the full Senate on February 2, 2010.

for.name: 3 of 58 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all three cosponsors were Democrats.

for.name: President Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Pressed Congress during 2009-2010 to pass comprehensive climate and energy legislation capping carbon emissions.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote; by mid-2010 announced the Senate would pursue a narrower energy bill instead of cap-and-trade.

against.name: Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Led united Senate Republican opposition to cap-and-trade legislation, which never gained a single Republican cosponsor.

against.name: Coal-state and moderate Senate Democrats
against.role: A bloc of roughly a dozen Democratic senators from coal and manufacturing states
against.what_they_did: Withheld support for a floor vote, leaving leadership short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster.

sides.party_line_note: All three cosponsors were Democrats, the bill was reported from a Democratic-run committee with minority views filed in opposition, and the legislation never attracted Republican support before it expired.

industries.note: New coal-fired plants would have to cut carbon dioxide emissions 50% (units permitted through 2019) or 65% (from 2020), and power plants would need allowances for their emissions — but the bill also allocates allowance value to merchant coal and electricity consumers and funds carbon capture and storage demonstration, with utilities assessing themselves through a new Carbon Storage Research Corporation to fund it. Utilities in coal-heavy regions bear the compliance burden while receiving free allowances and transition funding.

Fuel producers and importers are covered entities that must hold allowances, but the bill grants compensatory allowances for non-emissive uses of petroleum and allocates allowance value to domestic fuel production including small-business refiners. Consumers ultimately bear the fuel price impact of the cap.

The bill directs allowance value and auction proceeds to renewable energy deployment, clean vehicle technology manufacturing grants, advanced biofuels, building retrofits, and Energy Innovation Hubs — creating customers and revenue for the sector.

The bill declares it U.S. policy to grow the nuclear industry, funds nuclear worker training and research on plant safety and waste management, and directs allowance value to nuclear workforce programs — supporting an already-subsidized incumbent energy source.

Emission allowances and offset credits could be bought, sold, banked, and held by anyone in the country, not just regulated firms, creating a new nationwide commodity market with quarterly auctions and a market stability reserve. The bill creates oversight for this market but does not restrict participation.

Steel, chemicals, cement, and similar sectors would receive emission allowance rebates to shield them from the compliance costs their foreign competitors avoid, with the rebates phased out over ten years beginning in 2026.
